explanation: During Metaphase I, tetrads align randomly along the midline of the cell, with each homologous pair oriented randomly toward either spindle pole. Spindle fibers from opposite poles attach to the centromeres of the respective homologous chromosomes. In Anaphase I, the homologous chromosomes are pulled apart and move to opposite poles of the cell. This separates the tetrad, leaving sister chromatids joined at their centromeres (unlike in mitotic anaphase, where sister chromatids separate). This random segregation of maternal and paternal homologous chromosomes is called independent assortment, which contributes to genetic variation.

questions.q: How does chromosome separation in Anaphase I differ from mitosis?
opts: Homologous chromosomes are separated in Anaphase I, while sister chromatids remain joined; in mitosis, sister chromatids separate.
Sister chromatids are separated in Anaphase I, while homologous chromosomes remain joined; in mitosis, tetrads separate.
Chromosomes are degraded in Anaphase I; they are replicated in mitosis.
Spindle fibers do not attach to centromeres in Anaphase I; they attach in mitosis.
questions.exp: Option A is correct because the slide states: 'Tetrad is separated; not sister chromatids as in mitosis' under Anaphase I.
